title: Gethsemani, December 1941
hook: he enters a silent Cistercian abbey in the Kentucky hills

segments.voice: Yesterday, a convert in New York: a book, some friends, one quiet Mass, and a baptism. Your line was someone was drawing him. What's drawing you? Three years later, it draws him somewhere very quiet. Day two hundred seventy-four.

December 1941. The whole country is loud. Pearl Harbor has just been bombed, and every radio is talking about war. A twenty-six-year-old English teacher gets off a train in Kentucky, in the dark, with a small suitcase. He's given away most of what he owns. He rides out through frozen hills to a gate in a stone wall, and he rings the bell. On the other side, men pray through the night, work the fields, and barely speak. He'll live there the rest of his life. Today: into the silence.
screen: `DECEMBER 1941. A LOUD COUNTRY.` → `A GATE IN THE KENTUCKY HILLS.` → `INTO THE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the place. The Abbey of Our Lady of Gethsemani, near Bardstown, Kentucky. It was founded in 1848 by monks from France, and it's named for the garden where Jesus prayed the night before he died. Merton had made a retreat there that spring, in Holy Week, and wrote that it was the center of America. He arrived to stay on December 10, 1941. Second, the name. The monks are Cistercians of the Strict Observance, nicknamed Trappists after the abbey of La Trappe in France, where a seventeenth-century reform called monks back to a hard, simple life. They follow the Rule of Saint Benedict, written in the sixth century: prayer, work, reading, and a lot of quiet. Third, the silence. In Merton's day, Trappists spoke almost never. They used a simple sign language for work. They ate no meat, slept in their habits, and rose in the middle of the night to sing. Here's the surprise: there's no vow of silence. Their vows are obedience, stability, staying in one community for life, and conversion of life. Silence isn't a rule for its own sake. It's room. The Douay-Rheims puts it in one line from Lamentations: "It is good to wait with silence for the salvation of God." Fourth, the new life. Merton got a new name, Brother Louis. The loud, funny, restless young man had found a place where he could finally stop talking and listen. He wouldn't stay quiet on paper, as we'll see. But he stayed.
screen: `OUR LADY OF GETHSEMANI, KENTUCKY.` · `TRAPPISTS, AFTER LA TRAPPE.` · `NO VOW OF SILENCE, BUT ROOM.` · `A NEW NAME: BROTHER LOUIS.` · then, large: `IT IS GOOD TO WAIT WITH SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a little silence. For the next two minutes, no sound you make on purpose. Put the phone face down. Don't hum, don't narrate. Just let the room be as it is: the fridge, a car outside, your breath. When your mind starts talking, let it talk, and don't answer. That's the monks' secret: silence isn't empty, it's attention. If you pray, let this be the whole prayer. Later today, try to find five minutes more. The bell holds the time.
Trappist. A monk or nun of the Cistercians of the Strict Observance, named for the abbey of La Trappe. Prayer, work, and deep quiet. Today's word.
Your line: into the silence. Today, find five minutes with nothing playing, nothing scrolling, nobody talking. Treat it as room, not as nothing. Day two hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Trappist monks and nuns still live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, rising in the night for prayer, and many monasteries, including Gethsemani, welcome guests on silent retreats.
